title: Ἀετὸς καὶ ἀλώπηξ
part: The Eagle and the Fox (Chambry 3 · Perry 1)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 3 (= Perry 1). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀετὸς καὶ ἀλώπηξ φιλίαν πρὸς ἀλλήλους ποιησάμενοι πλησίον ἑαυτῶν οἰκεῖν διέγνωσαν, βεβαίωσιν φιλίας τὴν συνήθειαν ποιούμενοι.
sentences.tr: Aetos kai alōpēx philian pros allēlous poiēsamenoi plēsion heautōn oikein diegnōsan, bebaiōsin philias tēn synētheian poioumenoi.
sentences.l: An eagle and a fox, having made friendship with one another, decided to dwell near each other, making close company the confirmation of the friendship.
sentences.i: An eagle and a fox struck up a friendship and resolved to live near one another, making their constant company the pledge of it.
sentences.n: ποιησάμενοι … ποιούμενοι: the middle of ποιέω twice — first aorist for the pact once made, then present for the securing that was to go on. φιλίαν ποιεῖσθαι is the ordinary Greek for 'form a friendship'; the second participle takes two accusatives, making τὴν συνήθειαν (their close company) into βεβαίωσιν (the confirmation).

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ ὁ μὲν ἀναβὰς ἐπί τι περίμηκες δένδρον ἐνεοττοποιήσατο· ἡ δὲ εἰσελθοῦσα εἰς τὸν ὑποκείμενον θάμνον ἔτεκεν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē ho men anabas epi ti perimēkes dendron eneottopoiēsato· hē de eiselthousa eis ton hypokeimenon thamnon eteken.
sentences.l: And so he, having gone up onto a certain very tall tree, made his nest; and she, having gone into the bush lying beneath, gave birth.
sentences.i: So the eagle went up into a very tall tree and nested there, while the fox went into the thicket below and had her young.
sentences.n: ὁ μέν … ἡ δέ, 'the one … the other': the bare article carrying μέν and δέ does the work of pronouns, and the genders alone tell you eagle (masculine) from fox (feminine). ἐνεοττοποιήσατο, 'made itself a nest in it,' from νεοττός, 'nestling' — Greek builds long transparent compounds like this freely, and they are usually easier than they look.

sentences.t: Ἐξελθούσης δὲ αὐτῆς ποτὲ ἐπὶ νομήν, ὁ ἀετός, ἀπορῶν τροφῆς, καταπτὰς εἰς τὸν θάμνον καὶ τὰ γεννήματα ἀναρπάσας, μετὰ τῶν ἑαυτοῦ νεοττῶν κατεθοινήσατο.
sentences.tr: Exelthousēs de autēs pote epi nomēn, ho aetos, aporōn trophēs, kataptas eis ton thamnon kai ta gennēmata anarpasas, meta tōn heautou neottōn katethoinēsato.
sentences.l: And she having gone out once for pasture, the eagle, being at a loss for food, having swooped down into the bush and having snatched up her offspring, feasted upon them with his own nestlings.
sentences.i: Once when she had gone out foraging, the eagle, short of food, swooped down into the thicket, carried off her cubs, and made a feast of them with his own young.
sentences.n: A genitive absolute (Ἐξελθούσης … αὐτῆς) sets the moment, and then the aorist-participle chain runs — swooped, snatched — into a single finite verb at the very end. This is the standard shape of an Aesopic sentence: the participles carry the action, the main verb lands last. ἀπορέω takes the genitive of the thing lacked (τροφῆς).

sentences.t: Ἡ δὲ ἀλώπηξ ἐπανελθοῦσα, ὡς ἔγνω τὸ πραχθέν, οὐ ⟨τοσοῦτον⟩ ἐπὶ τῷ τῶν νεοττῶν θανάτῳ ἐλυπήθη ὅσον ἐπὶ τῇ ἀμύνῃ· χερσαία γὰρ οὖσα πετεινὸν διώκειν ἠδυνάτει.
sentences.tr: Hē de alōpēx epanelthousa, hōs egnō to prachthen, ou ⟨tosouton⟩ epi tōi tōn neottōn thanatōi elypēthē hoson epi tēi amynēi· chersaia gar ousa peteinon diōkein ēdynatei.
sentences.l: And the fox, having come back, when she learned the thing done, was grieved not ⟨so much⟩ at the death of her young as at the requital; for being a land creature she was unable to pursue a winged one.
sentences.i: When the fox came back and learned what had been done, she grieved not so much for the death of her cubs as for the vengeance — for a creature of the land could not pursue a creature of the air.
sentences.n: ⟨τοσοῦτον⟩ is Chambry's supplement, added to complete the pairing οὐ … ὅσον, 'not so much … as'; the angle brackets mark words absent from the transmitted text. τὸ πραχθέν, 'the thing done,' is the ordinary Greek way of saying 'what had happened.' ἐπὶ τῇ ἀμύνῃ is compressed and the sense has to be filled in: her grief is over requital — over her being unable to take it. ἀμύνη is a rare noun, roughly 'defence, retaliation,' and how much has been left out here is a matter of judgement.

sentences.t: Διόπερ πόρρωθεν στᾶσα, ὃ μόνον τοῖς ἀδυνάτοις καὶ ἀσθενέσιν ὑπολείπεται, τῷ ἐχθρῷ κατηρᾶτο.
sentences.tr: Dioper porrōthen stasa, ho monon tois adynatois kai asthenesin hypoleipetai, tōi echthrōi katērato.
sentences.l: Wherefore, having stood at a distance — the one thing that is left to the powerless and the weak — she kept cursing her enemy.
sentences.i: So she stood far off and cursed her enemy, which is all that is left to the helpless and the weak.
sentences.n: καταράομαι takes the dative of the person cursed (τῷ ἐχθρῷ). The relative ὅ stands in apposition to the whole act of cursing, not to any one noun — English does the same with 'which.' A curse was not merely bitter words: it called the gods down on the offender, and the rest of the fable is that call being answered.

sentences.t: Συνέβη δ’ αὐτῷ τῆς εἰς τὴν φιλίαν ἀσεβείας οὐκ εἰς μακρὰν δίκην ὑποσχεῖν· θυόντων γάρ τινων αἶγα ἐπ’ ἀγροῦ, καταπτὰς ἀπὸ τοῦ βωμοῦ σπλάγχνον ἔμπυρον ἀνήνεγκεν· οὗ κομισθέντος ἐπὶ τὴν καλιάν, σφοδρὸς ἐμπεσὼν ἄνεμος ἐκ λεπτοῦ καὶ παλαιοῦ κάρφους λαμπρὰν φλόγα ἀνῆψε.
sentences.tr: Synebē d’ autōi tēs eis tēn philian asebeias ouk eis makran dikēn hyposchein· thyontōn gar tinōn aiga ep’ agrou, kataptas apo tou bōmou splanchnon empyron anēnenken· hou komisthentos epi tēn kalian, sphodros empesōn anemos ek leptou kai palaiou karphous lampran phloga anēpse.
sentences.l: And it befell him not long after to undergo justice for his impiety against the friendship; for some people sacrificing a goat in the country, he swooped down and carried up from the altar a piece of burning entrails; and this having been brought to the nest, a violent wind falling on it kindled from a thin old straw a bright flame.
sentences.i: And before long he paid the penalty for that offence against friendship. Some people were sacrificing a goat out in the fields; he swooped down and carried off from the altar a piece of the burning entrails; and when he had brought it to his nest, a violent gust of wind caught it and kindled a bright flame out of a dry old wisp of straw.
sentences.n: δίκην ὑποσχεῖν, 'to undergo justice,' is the standard phrase for paying a penalty; οὐκ εἰς μακράν, 'not to a long (stretch),' means before long. Two more genitive absolutes, the second (οὗ κομισθέντος) with a relative pronoun as its subject — 'this having been carried' — where English starts a fresh clause with 'and when it…'. The σπλάγχνα are the inner organs of the victim, roasted on the altar fire and shared out among the worshippers as the first act of the feast; so what the eagle snatches is taken off the burning altar itself, still alight. ἀσέβεια is a religious word: not a breach of trust but an impiety.

sentences.t: Καὶ διὰ τοῦτο καταφλεχθέντες οἱ νεοττοὶ (καὶ γὰρ ἦσαν ἔτι ἀτελεῖς οἱ πτηνοί) ἐπὶ τὴν γῆν κατέπεσον.
sentences.tr: Kai dia touto kataphlechthentes hoi neottoi (kai gar ēsan eti ateleis hoi ptēnoi) epi tēn gēn katepeson.
sentences.l: And because of this the nestlings, burnt up (for they were still unformed, the winged ones), fell down to the ground.
sentences.i: And so the nestlings were scorched and fell to the ground — for they were as yet unfledged.
sentences.n: The parenthesis is the fable telling you why the chicks could not save themselves: ἀτελεῖς, 'incomplete, not fully formed.' οἱ πτηνοί, 'the winged ones,' sits awkwardly after it — it reads either as a predicate ('still imperfect as fliers') or as a noun in apposition to οἱ νεοττοί; the phrasing as transmitted is odd, and all that is certain is that they could not yet fly. The parentheses are Chambry's punctuation, not the manuscripts'.

sentences.t: Καὶ ἡ ἀλώπηξ προσδραμοῦσα ἐν ὄψει τοῦ ἀετοῦ πάντας αὐτοὺς κατέφαγεν.
sentences.tr: Kai hē alōpēx prosdramousa en opsei tou aetou pantas autous katephagen.
sentences.l: And the fox, having run up, in the sight of the eagle devoured them all.
sentences.i: And the fox ran up and ate them all before the eagle's eyes.
sentences.n: ἐν ὄψει, 'within sight of' — the same phrase turns up in the Eagle and the Beetle, where an eagle again devours a helpless charge in full view of the one who cannot prevent it. κατα- in κατέφαγεν is perfective: ate them up, every one.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ φιλίαν παρασπονδοῦντες, κἂν τὴν τῶν ἠδικημένων ἐκφύγωσι κόλασιν δι’ ἀσθένειαν, ἀλλ’ οὖν γε τὴν ἐκ θεοῦ τιμωρίαν οὐ διακρούονται.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi philian paraspondountes, kan tēn tōn ēdikēmenōn ekphygōsi kolasin di’ astheneian, all’ oun ge tēn ek theou timōrian ou diakrouontai.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who break faith with friendship, even if they escape the punishment of the wronged through weakness, still at any rate do not fend off the vengeance that comes from god.
sentences.i: The story shows that those who betray a friendship may escape punishment at the hands of the ones they wronged, if these are too weak to inflict it, but they do not fend off the vengeance that comes from heaven.
sentences.n: κἄν is καὶ ἐάν run together by crasis, 'even if,' with the subjunctive ἐκφύγωσι; the answering ἀλλ’ οὖν γε is 'still, in any case.' τῶν ἠδικημένων is a perfect participle used as a noun, 'those who have been wronged,' and δι’ ἀσθένειαν is their weakness, not the offenders'. παρασπονδέω is to break a σπονδή, a treaty sealed by libation — the friendship is treated as a sworn compact, which is why its breach is impiety.
